text:
"Nintendo NEVER cared about Zelda's story"

"Nintendo NEVER cared about the story" is a common refrain in discussions about the Zelda series, and while I know I'm probably preaching to the converted here I wanted to write out some thoughts about it.

Here are a few quotes from a 2007 Wired interview with Yoshiaki Koizumi:

…my ambition had always been to make drama. That was my goal: Having a character, in a certain kind of world, having him go through a series of actions to accomplish something, and creating a dramatic tension throughout that. And games seemed like a really good opportunity to create a kind of drama that you don't find in films.

EAD doesn't tend to focus on the big story in most of their games. But I was the one coming up with scenarios, just on my own, ever since the time of Link's Awakening. But even at that time, I felt like I came up with this entire scenario and a backstory for Link, but nobody really seemed to care. They were always saying, let's not try to push the story forward too much.

So I would sort of try to find sneaky ways to get it in without them noticing too much. For example, I always liked the idea of you coming upon another character and hearing little bits of conversation that slowly begin to reveal different parts of the story. And that was the way that I tried to work on Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask.

A brief summary of Koizumi's Zelda credits:
Wrote the manual and backstory for A Link to the Past
Designer/writer of Link's Awakening
Designer/director of Ocarina of Time and Majora's Mask (alongside Eiji Aonuma)
Assistant director of Wind Waker

Worth highlighting that many of the major plot elements Zelda fans like theorizing about (ex. the timeline split) come from these games. Also worth pointing out that some of the games that generate the most discussion about their themes/meaning/etc. (Link's Awakening, Majora's Mask) had heavy involvement from Koizumi.

My point here is not that Koizumi is the sole auteur responsible for Zelda having a story in spite of Nintendo. Koizumi IS Nintendo. Nintendo games are made by many different people with varying interests and priorities. I think it's likely that others who have played key roles in the development of Zelda games have had feelings about story closer to Koizumi's than Miyamoto's.

To be clear, you don't have to think any Zelda game's story is good. You don't have to care about the stories. You're free to speculate that a specific Zelda game was made by people who didn't care about its story. You can even be skeptical about whether the overarching continuity between Zelda stories is being cared for - that's a separate conversation.

What you can't do is tell people that nobody involved in making any Zelda game ever cared about story. You can't tell people they're delusional for noticing and caring about story in these games, or pretend that it's all fanfiction that Nintendo has been cowed into playing along with. You can't accuse people of being unreasonable for expecting or wanting story elements in Zelda games to reflect that the people who worked on them did, in fact, care.

text:
Bite-sized Zelda games

A good while back I floated the idea that Nintendo could continue serving us new 2D Zelda games through a theoretical Zelda Maker. Zelda Maker could come with a small Zelda game built using the included assets and made by the Nintendo team. Whenever they released DLC with new assets and features to be used in the Maker, a new, bite-sized Zelda would be released alongside it. Instead of ~$60 for a new full fat 2D Zelda every few years (or, as of late, never) it would be ~$20 every year or two for a small Zelda game, packaged with the new maker assets. What kind of games would you want to see if we started getting more frequent bite-sized releases instead of infrequent larger games? Would you want each of these games to be a totally standalone adventure with a new Link? Should the games all be part of a single, continuous series following the story of one Link? Or would you rather each game continue the story of another hero we've already met? Personally, I think it could be really interesting to have an 'epilogue' for games we've played like Twilight Princess or Skyward Sword, where we get to see what happens to those characters next. It would mesh well with the concept of releasing a new set of unique assets with each game, matching the art style of the source game. On the other hand, establishing brand new stories can be better than living in the past. And it's always possible to retroactively spoil a satisfying story by tacking more onto it.

text:
If Nintendo made another game set in the Adult Timeline, would you care if they went back on its progression?

To me, the Adult Timeline is the progress timeline, where the status quo actually changes. The first game in the timeline starts with Hyrule flooded, and the conclusion is that Hyrule, as least as we know it, isn't restored. Tetra and Link set off for new horizons, but old Hyrule is done.

This continues in Phantom Hourglass. Ganon doesn't make a return, Bellum doesn't turn to the camera and say 'I'm actually working for Ganon btw', and the game isn't even set in a flooded Hyrule.

Spirit Tracks has a Hyrule, but it's a new Hyrule. They have trains, the Triforce isn't relevant at all beyond holdover symbols, and the villain still isn't Ganon. You can make the argument that maybe Malladus is connected to Demise's curse somehow, but the evidence isn't necessarily conclusive, at least not as far as I can tell.

Instead of a vague connection, each game has a solid progression. Things have not reset, but have evolved from the entry the preceded it. It's not some award-winning, deep story, but it does feel like a tighter connection between games than we usually see in Zelda.

I, for one, do not want this pattern to be reversed. If they ever do make another Zelda game set in the Adult Timeline, I don't want Ganon or Ganondorf to return in even the vaguest capacity. I don't even know that I want the Triforce to be mentioned, and the Wild games further show that it doesn't need to be in every game.

If a new Zelda game in the Adult Timeline defaults back to the status quo, I'd actually rather there just never be another Adult Timeline game. For a game like that, there's nothing to be gained from placing it specifically in the Adult Timeline as opposed to the Downfall Timeline or the Child Timeline, or even just not acknowledging a timeline at all. If progression is untenable, then I'd rather let the Adult Timeline be forever left on a good note with Spirit Tracks.

But those are just my ramblings. What are your thoughts on the matter?
label: franchise_discussion

text:
Website Timeline Update and The “Shared Epilogue”

So, when the timeline updated on the Japanese Zelda site, many (including the YouTuber Zeltik) were excited to see that within the website's source code, the Wild era games (BotW and TotK) were categorized as a "shared epilogue" at the end of all three timelines.

Many fans have taken this as a potential confirmation of the "convergence" theory—the idea that somehow, somewhere down the line, all three timelines merged into one before the events of Breath of the Wild. 

However, looking at it from a web development and structural perspective, calling it a "shared epilogue" is literally just a functional CSS/code tag used to display the Wild era games universally at the bottom of the page regardless of which timeline path you scroll down.

What would this mean for Hyrule? The first convergence would be about reconciling different histories. The second would be about reconciling, or confronting, different realities. That raises an interesting question: can these worlds coexist without one having to erase or overwrite the others?
label: franchise_discussion

text:
Replaying MM3D, the worst change is still clearly Zora Link swimming

On a whim, I elected to charge up my 3DS and bring it with me on a recent international trip, which turned out to be a damn good decision, as we got stuck for 5 days with nothing to do.

Started a new save in MM3D and, given that there's been years since my last playthrough, I've had a lot of distance to assuage some of my prickliness at the changes in the remake.

I really like the remake on my second playthrough. Almost all of the noticeable changes made by Grezzo make a lot of sense to me and don't offend me any longer. The one change that still stands out as really terrible, however, is how they changed Zora Link swimming. Making the "power" swim movement tied to the barrier use really sucks, since the movement in the original was super fun. Being able to zip around the sea and pop out like a dolphin was very cool in the N64 version.

Not sure what the cause of the change was, but it makes Zora Link and the Great Bay parts of the game less fun.

The best change outside of how time and saving works has to be moving Shiro from the Ikana Canyon road to the middle of the Pirate Fortress. That's a brilliant change that just makes sense.

All in all, Zora Link swimming mechanics being the worst change means the remake was exceptionally well-done and the QoL changes to passage of time and saving make the remake superior to the original.
